utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could we call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, good afternoon to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. General Talic, good afternoon to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Joanna Korner, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager. Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm John Ackerman, along with Marela Jevtovic for Mr. Brdjanin. Good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you. Appearances for General Talic. MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] Mr. President, my name is Xavier de Roux, and Natasha Fauveau-Ivanovic for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Any preliminaries?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours, I'm very sorry but I'm going to have to go back to the question of the 90(H) yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. We can hear the counsel for Defence very poorly. Could she perhaps raise the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your voice is not reaching the interpreters well enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will approach the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was very surprised yesterday when Ms. Korner said -- and I'm going to quote her words in order to avoid interpretation that could be erroneous. [In English] If General Talic, were he to give evidence, were going to say in evidence, "I did not use those words," then it must be put to the witness that he's either mistaken or lying when he says that General Talic used those words. [Interpretation] Unfortunately, yesterday I did not have your decision with me. However, I do know what you wrote in this decision. And now I've got it. And in the paragraph 14, on page 6 -- I believe that is page 7 in the English version -- the Chamber has decided that it is good to underline, however, that there is no absolute rule or general rule that can oblige the Defence counsel to give --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. We do not have the decision in front of us, the English version in front of us. It is --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In light of this decision, I would like to ask the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The interpreters, because they don't have the English, are having a great deal of difficulty in following. If you could -- do Your Honours have the motion with you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course not. I wasn't prepared to -- for this. I mean, we were not told, except just before I walked in, that Madam Fauveau was going to raise something related to 90(H). Otherwise, I didn't come -- I don't come here with all the previous decisions and rulings of this Chamber, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We've got -- can I hand up our copy?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if Madam Fauveau could read the English version, it's probably easier for the interpreters. Oh, I see you're going to read the English yourself, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will now reread it in English. [In English] "It should be pointed out, however, that there is no absolute or general rule requiring Defence counsel to put to the Prosecution the accused's version of the events or to put the witness on notice of every date the Defence counsel does not accept."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, in the light of this decision, I cannot see why I should be obliged to present to the witness the words of General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think, Madam Fauveau, again, once more - and I am not going to reopen the discussion - you are misunderstanding completely the whole concept behind our decision and behind the rationale of Rule 90(H). You are not requested to tell the witness what your client is going to testify if he -- if he testifies, or if he decides to testify. If there is something which -- well, I'm not going to say more. I'm sorry, I'm not going to say more. What we had to say, we said it in our decision, which is now subject to appeal and --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not going to tell you or Mr. Ackerman how you should conduct your cross-examination in the light of our decision on 90(H). That's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think all one can -- I see Maitre de Roux is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Again, I'm sorry, on one particular matter under discussion, only one counsel will be allowed to make representations, not two. I cannot allow Madam Fauveau to stand up and make submissions and then allow you to stand up to make submissions on the same. Decide amongst yourself who is going to make submissions, but only one counsel will be allowed to make submissions on a specific matter. MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we are a defence team, and you know that well, and I believe that there are problems of principle. I think that there are problems of principle that are being presented in the procedures before the Tribunal and where it is necessary to intervene. And now, I don't have any problem with your interpretation and with your decision. Your decision is extremely clear. I have a problem with the Prosecution, which is always putting into question the decision that you have issued. As far as I'm concerned, I am perfectly satisfied with the interpretation given by the Tribunal, which seems to me perfectly in accordance with Rule 90(H), and what I'm saying, I'm not saying this for you, Mr. President, I'm saying this for the Prosecution, for Ms. Korner, and paragraph (H) says that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, stop, Maitre de Roux. Stop. I am not going to allow any further discussion on 90(H). That matter has been decided by this Trial Chamber. There is an appeal pending and it will be decided by the Court of Appeal. In the meantime, what was stated yesterday stays, remains. The matter is not open for further discussion, neither from your side nor from Mr. Ackerman's side nor from Ms. Korner's side, and we proceed with the -- any other further preliminaries that you may have.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I propose that we conclude with this witness's testimony and then raise the matters before moving on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you do, I don't know if you are aware of the decision which was handed down by Trial Chamber II in Stakic this morning regarding 7.35.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In that we can disclose the transcripts, yes. However, the witness is leaving today at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. But I wanted to make sure --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm aware of that decision. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We may go into closed session now, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we move now to Sanski Most, may I, as it were, deal with a few matters that are connected with still the Banja Luka municipality and then how we see this case going? The first thing, Your Honour, is that we have not yet, in fact, dealt with quite a lot of the documents that are in binder -- volumes 2, 3 and 4 of the Banja Luka documents, but I have a witness here and I'm anxious, as I'm sure Your Honours are, to move on. We haven't completed the Banja Luka municipality for a number of reasons. We still have the witnesses from the humanitarian organisation; we still have Colonel Selak, who, although in fact he's going to come in when and if we ever reach Prijedor in this case; there is also the witness who is going to deal with the diary, and I think the translation is more or less now sorted. Just for the record, as Your Honour knows, we, as it were, selected what we thought remained that ought to be translated, excised some of the stuff that seemed to us to be completely irrelevant. The defence know about it, so unless they've got --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let her finish, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So unless they've got in touch with CLSS to say they want more translated than we've indicated, all that will be translated is what we've indicated, but that's the rest of the diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are working on that process. The list that we got from the Prosecutor was -- it's like the same complaint Ms. Korner has about some of the things I give her. They told us the things that they were going to translate rather than the things that they weren't so we have to now go through day after day after day and find what it is they have not designated for translation to determine whether or not there is material in there we think must be translated. We are engaged in that process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we depend entirely on the three of you - on you, Mr. Ackerman, on Maitre de Roux, and on you, Ms. Korner - because you have assistance in having someone who knows the Serbo-Croat language to -- while we don't. So we depend entirely on you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It doesn't come from me. It comes from people who help me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And he will clearly not be called before September of this year, when we are told the diary translation will be complete. So in a sense, and it's -- perhaps it fits in with the general tenor of the case. Banja Luka runs -- will run through the rest of this case. Associated with that, as Your Honours know, because I raised, or associated with Banja Luka, Mr. Dzonlic provided his documents. I cannot resist saying this in open court, in the light of Mr. Ackerman's comment. There were some 13 dismissal letters. Five in terms state that the dismissals are occasioned by the ARK Crisis Staff decision of the 22nd of June, but we suddenly realised that today was the last day. Your Honours said 14 days. They've been here for a week so I'm just saying that they will be given to Mr. Ackerman and to General Talic's team tomorrow. Your Honour, that brings me on to the general progress of the case. Banja Luka we knew would take some time because the witnesses are all, as it were, dealing with (a), the -- particularly Mr. Brdjanin and the events in Banja Luka. And none were specifically crime-base, that is, describing events that happened to them. Your Honour, we, in the interests of, we hope, good management and efficiency, have taken another look at the case over the last few weeks, in particular whether we feel that it is in the interests of good case management, efficiency, and necessity to call all the evidence that we indicated we would call. In particular, we have taken a decision that in relation to five particular municipalities - which I will now name so that the Defence and Your Honours are aware in advance - we are going to drastically reduce the evidence, both in terms of the documents and the witnesses who are listed. Those are as follows, in alphabetical, as opposed to the order which they may be set out in the indictment: First of all, Bosanska Dubica. There will be no more than two witnesses called. If necessary, I can tell Your Honours the -- the numbers of the witnesses, and my learned friends at this stage, though we're some distance off. I'm in the Court's hands on that. In respect of Bosanska Gradiska, one witness. In respect of Donji Vakuf, two witnesses. In respect of Ripac, one witness -- Ripac-Bihac. And in respect of Sipovo, two witnesses only. And Your Honours, I can say the documents for those municipalities don't even -- we will give a full list eventually or before we get there. They will be -- have already been reduced to something less than one binder for all those municipalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And how does this -- because I wasn't expecting this, obviously, and therefore, I do not have the documents before me. How does this compare with what you had intended or told us --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, in respect of those municipalities, I think we listed something in the region of four or five witnesses plus some Rule 92. It's almost certain we won't even be applying for Rule 92. Effectively, the concentration of this case, we feel, both from the view of the Defence and of Your Honours, should be on the -- what we've listed as the five or six major municipalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. What I suggest to you are two things, Ms. Korner. First, I think that the Defence teams would be interested or should be provided with the names of the witnesses that you intend to bring forward in these five --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I can do that right now. I'll just give their numbers. In respect of Dubica, 7.9 and 7.104 will be called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In respect of Gradiska, 7.126. In respect of Donji Vakuf, 7.159 and 7.156. In respect of Ripac, 7.71. And in respect of Sipovo, 7.176 and 7.116. Your Honour, in addition, it's -- the evidence on Prnjavor will not be much longer than that, but there are -- it's slightly more complicated because of the military aspect to that municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How would this reflect -- the second thing was this one: How would this reflect on the length of the case for the Prosecution? In other words, would --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it will certainly knock some time off. We're rather in the hands of the Defence on the length of cross-examination, appreciating that up till now the evidence in chief has normally been -- not always, but normally been longer because of the documents. And as I think I said to Your Honour yesterday, the next witness for Sanski Most will be a very lengthy witness because effectively he can deal with just about every document going, for reasons that Your Honour will hear. After that, the evidence will be much, much shorter in each witness because it relates to a particular crime or set of crimes. And really there is no other witness that for the moment I can bring to mind from any other municipality who's going to be quite as lengthy as this witness is going be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Would the Defence like to put in some remarks, comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm wondering if Ms. Korner might be able to elaborate just a little bit on how she sees this affecting the time. For instance, does she believe that the Prosecutor's case can be completed during this calendar year? Because it would make a difference to our efforts whether we -- the Prosecutor's case is going to take another nine months or 12 months. Until I know that, it will affect how I have to deal with getting my case ready to go, basically.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that's the difficulty. I could make an educated guess and say that if cross-examination were limited, the answer is yes, we would finish by the end of this calendar year. It depends on breaks, on events like Mr. Ackerman has described happening in Banja Luka, as far as his team is concerned, adjournments. Were we to sit throughout, between now and the end of the year, with just having the break in the summer, the answer is probably yes, but it's terribly difficult to guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And perhaps after the next meeting you have with Mr. Von Hebel, the picture should be even better.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think, Your Honour, given the meetings this Thursday - and I'm not sure what the point of the meeting is any more, because effectively, we have given Your Honour the information. We provided the chart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's true, but Ms. Korner, we were also a little bit, not exactly sceptical but almost, before the first of such meetings was held, and we all came to the conclusion that it was very positive and I think I would stick to that procedure, because first of all, the informal atmosphere is conducive to your cooperating more with one another, and also in bringing out the problems that besiege this trial from time to time, so ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, I would say on balance, despite some of the remarks yesterday and today - and I'm as much to blame as the Defence - we are actually cooperating rather well on the whole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think you are; and one other thing I want to make clear, Ms. Korner, is that so far, at least, I cannot in all honesty criticise in the least the Defence in the way they have been conducting their cross-examination. It hasn't been too lengthy, too long, or beyond what one would expect in a case like this, and I think also it has been very professionally conducted so far, and I'm quite happy. Perhaps - and I have been seriously thinking about this over the past months - perhaps I might come to the conclusion that I would start intervening, stepping in, more than I have, both during the examination-in-chief and during cross-examination, to try and eliminate certain questions or curtail on certain questions, especially now that we have -- we are going into the fourth month in this trial and certain facts have already been mentioned by various witnesses and certain other facts made abundantly clear, in the opinion of the Tribunal, which would make it perhaps superfluous to have certain questions repeated and certain answers repeated. So don't be surprised if there comes a time very, very soon, when I will stop you from putting certain questions or say he doesn't need to answer it because the Chamber is satisfied that that answer -- that there is already enough information on -- I will try to do it as least as possible because my belief is the least I interfere, the better it is, but there may come a time when I will have to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would be most grateful for any indication the Trial Chamber cared to give that they don't require further evidence on any particular topic. And as Your Honour says, if Your Honour simply steps in and makes that clear, then we would be very grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then, Your Honour, there are still a few couple of matters. The first is - I just go back to it - Your Honour did say you might be able to tell us about May the 17th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I am able to tell you. I discussed it today. I don't think I -- we have the option. It was made abundantly clear to me that I'm expected to stick by the decision that has been taken by the bureau.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No breaking of ranks?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. So there won't be any sitting on the 17th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. That's very helpful from the point of view of witnesses. Your Honour, the only other thing is in respect of the Sanski Most Rule 92 application. I don't say it's particularly urgent, but I think Your Honour said you were expecting to give a ruling at some stage in the near future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just looking for -- yes. We will -- and I don't have the document in front of me at the moment, Ms. Korner, but we are definitely looking into that and we'll have it decided -- I don't know where I put it. We will have it decided in due course.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I'm grateful to Your Honour. Just we did have a request -- we made an error in saying that one witness supported another. And we've supplied -- or we were going to supply the statement today of the witness whose evidence the Rule 92 one supports. Your Honour, that's all I have to raise, unless there are any matters that Your Honour would wish to raise before we turn --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The only thing I wanted to raise was this: I found here -- I was given today a whole bundle of documents --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- plus two more documents which I understand are to replace two other documents with the same number that were inserted in our Banja Luka --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I gather, there was an error. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- the Sanski Most binders. That is -- okay. That is point taken. These others, this whole bundle, is this an extra --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is an extra binder, no?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, these are extra documents that the witness -- were attached to his statement effectively but weren't contained in the Banja Luka -- I'm doing it now -- Sanski Most binders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And may I ask you if these were all - without exception, in other words - included in the document that Mr. Inayat produced in the very beginning of this trial?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. These are documents that the witness -- the witness himself produced. Although, as Your Honours are going to hear, this particular witness is in fact the source of a number of documents that are in the Sanski Most binder. But in addition to that, when he was seen on the four or five different occasions, he himself produced extra documents which didn't go into the Sanski Most binders. So those are on top. Now, Your Honours, I should tell you I think some of them are a bundle of exhumation reports. He conducted them. Your Honour, although I wanted them all produced physically - because you never know when they may not become important - I'm only going to refer to selected parts of them with the witness as examples.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think -- I think it will become -- I'm sorry, in a sense it almost becomes simpler if we hand them out at the time the witness is going to refer to them rather than giving them all to Your Honours in advance. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I don't -- I don't have a problem with that. The only thing I want to make sure of is that the -- that the Defence have been given these documents, which I suppose they have.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: They got them with the statements, Your Honour, or through other disclosure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that there are no translation problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Not as far as I'm aware. I think some were disclosed last Friday. But unless I'm told differently, I don't think there are any translation problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think we got some documents within the last few days -- maybe the ones last Friday, the ones that she's talking about -- that were B/C/S only. We haven't got any English translations of any of those.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Some are -- some are just pure lists of names, which we didn't bother to translate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Those are -- and if that's all there is, I don't have any problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And in any case, as I understand, they need not necessarily be documents that we will be making use of.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. In particular, the list of names --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, the list of names is easy. It's not the problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, exactly. All the exhumation -- all the earlier stuff, which is the bulk of it, has been -- or a sample, at least, has been translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Ms. Korner. And I thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Since I haven't seen the pile of documents you've been handed, it's difficult for me to tell you whether or not I have them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Well, what I would invite you to do is that if there are problems, Mr. Ackerman, please let me know in good time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My assumption is that we have them. But the only way I could really be certain is if somebody would hand me a pile of them and I would spend, you know, a couple of hours going through them. But I think we have them all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. So can we bring the witness in now?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, please, Mr. Adil Draganovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's actually Judge Draganovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is he a current judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, he is a current judge. He was also President of the Tribunal before he was ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, could I ask when the next break is going to be, so I know when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The next break will be at 4.35 -- sorry, at 4.20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. More or less. I think this is a better system, having a 15-minute break every hour and 15 minutes rather than a break after two hours, because I keep my eyes wide open during the -- during the sitting and try to notice what -- what's going on, and apart from the interpreters, it's also the stenographers having to sit down two solid hours going that and -- I -- it must be very tiring. So I think we'll stick to the hour and 15 minutes and then a pause for 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Judge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The gentleman standing next to you is going to hand you a specimen solemn declaration to speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, and -- which you are kindly asked to make in this courtroom before you start your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and you may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sir, you being a judge, I need hardly explain the routine, the procedure here. We are the Chamber. I'm the Presiding Judge. To my right is Judge Janu from the Czech Republic, and to my left is Judge Taya from Japan. And it's more or less the procedure is similar to any other court of criminal jurisdiction. You will be asked questions first by the Prosecutor, who is to your right, and after that, the two teams, two Defence teams - one for Mr. Brdjanin, which is the one nearest to you, and followed by the Defence team for General Talic - will cross-examine you. The persons you see in front obviously are the registry. Ms. Korner will commence her examination-in-chief now. Should at any time -- should you at any time like to have a break, apart from the breaks that we will be having in the course of normality, please just let me know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, is your name Adil Draganovic?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And were you born on the 30th of August, 1952?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And are you a Muslim by ethnicity, now called Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And are you still at the moment the Court President, and therefore Judge, at the municipal court in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And were you originally appointed to that position in 1988?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You, as we are going to hear, were arrested in May of 1992, and kept in the Manjaca prison camp after a short period in the police station, until December of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was arrested, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And after December, 1992, did you leave the country?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you return to Sanski Most after it had been retaken by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in October of 1995?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you resume, eventually, your position in the court as the President?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did return, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Before I come to the various matters which you're going to deal with, I think it's right that you have in total made a number - one, two, three, four - four -- five statements to the Office of the Prosecutor. You probably don't remember.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And were you given an opportunity, before coming into Court, to refresh your memory from the contents of these statements?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And in addition, I think you've had a chance to look at some, if not all, of the documents that relate to the Sanski Most area?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I just want to make the position clear. I think this is right: You yourself were present in Sanski Most until June of 1992, when you were transported to Manjaca; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, until the 17th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But after your return to Sanski Most in 1995, effectively, you were in charge of the investigations into possible human rights violations and crimes that had been committed in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And by "within Sanski Most," I mean also within the municipality, as opposed to just the town.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And so as a result, have you seen a number of documents and, I suppose items is the way of describing it, as a result of your investigations?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I saw many documents that I believe to be evidence for the International Tribunal for War Crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I just want to make it clear to the Trial Chamber the sources of the evidence you're going to give. I think it's effectively three: Firstly, events which you witnessed yourself and were present at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Secondly, matters that people told you about that had happened after your arrest and whilst you were in Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then thirdly, matters that have come to your attention as a result of the investigations that you carried out after the Dayton Accords?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And just so that you understand, so it's important that when you give evidence about matters, you make it clear how you know about these matters and how you've come across various documents.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will say it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I think that you yourself submitted a number of documents and statements to the Office of the Prosecutor at this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And have you worked in liaison with the office of AID, both in Sanski Most and in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I cooperated with the AID.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then finally, I think, as part of your investigations, you were present at, and dealt with reports on, exhumations of effectively mass graves that were discovered really from late 1995 onwards?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And finally, before we begin on events, I forgot to mention you also, I think, made a number of statements to the German authorities in connection with proposed prosecutions that they were going to mount?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I gave a number of statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we just deal, then, sir, first of all, Judge, very briefly, with your background. I think that you went to Sarajevo University and studied law, graduating in 1975?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: After graduation, I think you worked for a small company and then did your mandatory military service in 1977?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I served my military service from 1977 to 1978 in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you actually serve with an anti-aircraft artillery unit of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And as a result of your service, did you become familiar with the weapons that were used by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting an expert, just familiar.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: As much as I could, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, subsequently, did you go to Bosanska Dubica and work as an assistant director to the local hospital for about four years?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then in Dubica, did you in fact become a judge and work with the municipal court there for about six years?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then in 1987, were you offered the opportunity to become a judge in the Sanski Most court?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: I mean, it's correct. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And after you'd been there for about a year, were you designated as the court President?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And as a result of that appointment, apart from your work within the court system itself, did you also deal with government and other official bodies of power and people in authority generally in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did some work in the municipality as an expert member of a municipal committee.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, before we go any further, I'd like you to be shown, please, and the Court, perhaps, to remind ourselves of where Sanski Most lies. Could you be shown --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I cannot remember whether we produced it, but it's the map of the Krajina area. Whether it has an exhibit number ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. P446.1, I'm told it is. And if the witness could have that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, if we just look at that -- the map, we see that the municipality of Prijedor lies to the north-eastish, I suppose, Banja Luka to the east, and then Kljuc to the south --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suppose, Ms. Korner, I suppose that if there is an extra copy which could be put on the ELMO, the video recording and everything would make more sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't realise Your Honours didn't have it there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The problem is not us having it or not having it. Since you are making specific references to the map, I suppose that if there is one on the ELMO, it can be captured on the video recording of the sitting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, thank you. Thank you very much, Your Honour. I keep forgetting there's going to be a video recording.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. We were saying -- I was saying, rather, Kljuc to the south -- sorry, west, and then Petrovac to the south, Krupa, Novi, and then Prijedor. So in fact Sanski Most now is in the centre of this Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. particular area. You can see marked on the map, sir, the various towns and villages, indicating whether they were largely, if not completely, either containing persons of Serb ethnicity or of Muslim or Croat. And would you agree that's -- that's roughly an accurate depiction? You can see the Muslim are in green; the Serb in blue, I think; and Croat in orange.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Yes, I can see it on the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How far away was the town of Sanski Most from Prijedor town?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Sanski Most is 28 kilometres away from Prijedor, and Prijedor is located to the north in relation to the Sanski Most municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, could you, while we're on the subject of maps, please be shown another map, this time the one -- and I think this is a new exhibit -- of the town of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it's one of the ones that we've prepared with photographs, Your Honour, of various places. Your Honour, I don't think this has been allocated an exhibit number yet, so -- we premarked the Sanski Most binders. So that will be 600 -- Well, Your Honour, what we did -- we still have some spare numbers going between 500 and whatever -- 47.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, exactly. That's what I understood.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was wondering whether it wouldn't be easier to keep Sanski Most starting at 600 and move upwards, even though there's some missing exhibit numbers, if you see what I mean. So I'm going to ask if we can -- all right. It may not be the clearest explanation -- if we can be given -- yeah. Anyhow, we'll be given the number in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, sir, can you look at this map.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And perhaps -- yes, that's been put on the ELMO. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Does that show a map of the town of Sanski Most, a plan?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is a map of the town of Sanski Most with the immediate surroundings.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, we can see --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And again, Your Honours, I should indicate these photographs were taken last year, so they're not the same -- I'm sorry, it isn't as it was in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: First of all, can we look at photograph number 7, which is the Mahala part of Sanski Most. Was that where you lived?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's where my house is, where I lived, and where I still live today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can we look at the photograph that was taken, as I say, last year. In 1992 -- sorry, perhaps the -- we may get some of the photographs brought in -- but did Mahala look much as it does in that photograph, it being rebuilt?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as the number of houses is concerned, or private houses, family houses, I think that the number is identical as in 1992. In 1992, the houses, more than 80 per cent of them were set on fire, destroyed, razed to the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: But after --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But it was rebuilt, as -- it was rebuilt, as I think we can see.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, that area of Sanski Most - we are going to hear about the various ethnicities in a moment - was it mixed ethnicity or just one particular ethnicity that lived there?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: In Sanski Most, several ethnicities lived; Muslims, Serbs, Croats, and there were other ethnicities as well. In total, the municipality had about 61.000 inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And in the settlement or the area of Mahala, was that mixed or was it one particular ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: In Mahala, Mahala was inhabited exclusively by Muslims, 100 per cent Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: While we are looking at the map, then, were there any areas in Sanski Most that were, for example, entirely Serb?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were such areas. For instance, the locality of Dabar, Kruhari, where there were also several Croatian houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I think we will have to get -- there is a third map but I'll come back to that one. Can we just look at, please, some of the areas that have been photographed? We'll leave out photograph number 1 for the time being because that will become more relevant when you've told us what happened. The SUP, the police station, did that look roughly the same in 1992 as we can see in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the building of SUP. It was also the building of the Secretariat for People's Defence in 1992, and today it looks the same as it did in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then again, I think we'll leave the other photographs. All right, could you be handed now, finally, a third map which shows Sanski Most with the places that you've just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could we get an exhibit number on this so that it is reflected in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Quite right. Could that be made Prosecutor's Exhibit 757, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner, and thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In fact, Your Honour, could that be made 757A and then the next map B so we keep the maps together, the one I'm about to hand out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We are using A and B to designate English and B/C/S, so we cannot do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right, yes, 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the next one will be 757.2. I'm sorry, Your Honour, I think Your Honour said -- no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we will break --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we need to break now. We will give this map its number, exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we will break for 15 minutes. We are going to have a short break, sir, and you will continue with your evidence immediately after.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may be -- I mean, this is not a protected witness. In future, if the witness is in court before Your Honours come in -- because the witness room is quite a long way away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you're right, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Judge, we were about to look at the map of the Sanski Most area itself. You talked about areas that were effectively Serb areas. And can we see those marked with purple -- in purple?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see this map of the Sanski Most municipality. I see that in green are areas principally inhabited by Muslims. I also see that red indicates some areas with the predominant Croat population, apart from Poljak, which had a mixed population, Muslims, Croats, and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: I also -- excuse me. I also note that blue indicates places with a predominant Serb population, although in some of these areas, the inhabitants were of mixed origin, such as Kljevci, Budimlic-Japra. Kasapnica is an area where there were no Serbs. In other such places, Serbs were the predominant population. So this is my answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you just indicate the one -- it may be well if you'd indicate on the ELMO with a pointer. Which was the one you say there were no Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, if he is going to indicate on the ELMO, please perhaps you could either move the ELMO nearer to him, if you can. I don't -- and -- And Judge, please -- exactly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I have said, the place called Kasapnica, at which I'm pointing now. As I have said, Badimlic-Japra -- where Muslims and Serbs both lived. Some parts of Badimlic-Japra were inhabited by Muslims and some others by Serbs. Poljak - and I'm pointing at it now - had a mixed population of Muslims, Croats, and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you're saying, are you -- would you say that the Croats were larger than the other two ethnicities in Poljak?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, no, I don't think I'd say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. So that -- in that case, that's misleading, I think. And could we go back to Kasapnica. Are you saying that there were no Serbs there? It wasn't a Serb village, as far as you were concerned?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Kasapnica was an area which the Croat population abandoned.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The Croat population.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know. I'd also like to add something as regards Poljak. I am not sure, because this is a suburban street which stretches as far as Sasina, so it is possible that there is a majority Croat population there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, sir. We'll do a double-check.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honour -- Your Honours, I think it's right that we just double-check those two places. I think we took that from statistics, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And also what I haven't really grasped is -- or understood is which town or village that he referred to before, where according to the witness there were absolutely no Serb population at all, because you seem to have understood like I did initially, that it was Kasapnica, but obviously it isn't. So perhaps the witness could tell us which village he was referring to earlier on in his evidence -- his testimony where there were no Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could you please repeat your question? Do you mean all the areas in the municipality of Sanski Most where there were no Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, sir. There was a point during your testimony where you were mentioning examples of towns and villages where there was either a predominance of one ethnicity or where there was a mixed community, and you also mentioned one village where, according to you, there were no Serbs at all. Which was that village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Kasapnica.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think we both understood that is correct, Your Honour, but we will check both those ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because this one is being marked as predominantly Serb. Okay. I thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As we can see - and we'll come to the exact figures for Sanski Most municipality later - there was a slight majority of Muslims within the municipality itself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: In the Sanski Most municipality, in -- according to the census of 1991, there were 47 per cent of Muslims, Serbs accounted for 41 per cent, and the Croat population accounted for 8 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. You can put the map aside now, thank you very much. Now, I want to come to the political events, really nationwide and within Sanski Most in particular. I think within Sanski Most, were you elected as the first president of the commission for the multi-party elections which took place in November of 1990?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is right. I was the chairman of the municipal election commission in Sanski Most, elected to conduct the first multi-party elections in the municipality of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then later on, were you also responsible for the legal administration of the referendum in respect of independence for Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The municipal election commission was duty-bound to organise and conduct the referendum in conformity with statute.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to deal, though, with the results of the 1990 elections. Did you see the results of the elections as published in the Official Gazette of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: I did. I saw them published, and these results were published on the basis of the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you -- yes, I'm sorry, of the report what? That was submitted from each municipality?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I think we can move on. I want to you look at, however, please, the Official Gazette for the result of the elections.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think Your Honour has already got a copy, and if -- it's not been made an exhibit yet, so that could be handed out to the witness in B/C/S. Your Honours, we have only -- the whole Gazette was translated but we've only copied the parts that are relevant to this case. Could that be made, then, Prosecutor's Exhibit 758, please? I think everybody else has got it, everybody else has got it, Mr. Usher. The defence have got it, unless they want another copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is 758?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 8, yes, and could the witness have the B/C/S copy, please. It should be at the back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is that a photocopy of the Official Gazette which you've had a chance to look at, I think, in advance?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It is the Official Gazette of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina which published the results.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to do the first part fairly quickly. There were, in fact, I think, seven constituencies.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, and we were a part of the Banja Luka constituency.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And we can see the parties that stood for these elections, or stood in these elections. The HDZ -- first of all, let's take it in order, the Democratic Social Alliance of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Banja Luka; the HDZ, the Croatian Democratic Union; the SDA, the Party of Democratic Action; then the Alliance of the Reform Forces of Yugoslavia, I think that was generally known as the Reform Party; something called the Democratic Alliance; and then the SDS. The other constituencies were Bihac, Doboj, Mostar and, in fact, Sarajevo and Tuzla and Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think we bothered to copy that but those were the seven.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we then come, please, to the page which is our page 4 of the translation where we look at the deputies elected in the constituencies? If you could find Banja Luka, sir -- sorry, I can't tell you what page it's on. I think it's under item 3; is that correct? You have that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. The Banja Luka constituency, again, as you say, it included Sanski Most. We can see just quickly, though, number 2 from Bosanska Gradiska, the candidate for the HDZ was somebody called Marijan Vistica.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm referring to that because that's -- the witness yesterday referred to him as the gentleman -- or the day before, or Friday -- as the man he met -- or the man, sorry, who was imprisoned. Then under the list of the SDS, Kupresanin, Kasagic, and Srlic -- I'm sorry, that's Prijedor, Banja Luka. Over the page -- I'm sorry. And I missed out -- I beg your pardon, sir. For Sanski Most, we can see somebody called Rasema Mehadzic?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Mehadzic. Yes, she represented the SDA. There is also Nedeljko Rasula.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Representing the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then if we go to the next page, we can see again under "Banja Luka," and number 11 there was Andjelko Grahovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Again, Your Honours, that's a name that's come up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we move, then, please, from that to -- we left in all the constituencies. If we go through that, to next page, page 9, which shows the national structure of the population of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, according to the 1981 census.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman and Maitre de Roux, are these figures in any way contested by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't think so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Maitre de Roux? MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... as well subject, of course, to the right of Defence counsel later on to ask questions -- put questions to the witness on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, then can we go -- I think it's the names that I need Your Honours to look at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, the names, I understand --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah, not the statistics.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we go, then, please, to page 11. And, sir, could you find the constituency of Banja Luka -- of the municipality of Banja Luka. It is the results of the elections by constituency. Have you found that? No, not quite yet, sir. It should be, I think -- it should start on the page with the number at the top 00497409. At least, I hope -- or the one before that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask for assistance from --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. You've found it. I'm grateful, sir.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you look at the municipality of the constituency of Banja Luka, we can see there the candidates for the SDS; that's Nikola Erceg. Then the Reform party; the HDZ, Dr. Kozic; and then for the SR BH, SDP, the Democratic Socialist Alliance, Dzevad Osmancevic. And we can see that in fact the deputy elected was Nikola Erceg.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we then -- could we move, then, please, to the next page, Bosanska Dubica.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm doing all of these so we don't have to go back to them.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Dubica.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Dubica. Do we see there that the SDS candidate, Mr. Slobodan Bijelic was elected?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Under 5? Yes, he was elected.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Could we then go to Gradiska.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we can do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And there we see that a Serb named Grbic was elected? And the following constituency, Bosanska Krupa. Suad Alibegovic, from the SDA party, was elected.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then if we go to the next one, Bosanski Novi, number 10 -- or the one after the next one. I'm sorry. Number 10, Bosanski Novi. A Serb was elected named Gakovic. Petrovac, number 11. Again a Serb, Dragan Milanovic, was elected.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. Under number 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's right. Then could we go to the next municipality -- we've missed some out. Sir, if you could go to -- I'm sorry. Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I may have missed it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. We've got -- the next one is Sarajevo. And I don't -- although I've actually left it in, I don't think we need that, that I've copied. If we look, however, at the next page, page 19. And if we come to Celinac, where we -- there we can see that in fact there were only -- the only people stood for election there were both Serbs, one for the SDS, one for the SDP, Democratic Socialist Alliance. And as we can see, Mr. Brdjanin was elected. If we go to the next page, Donji Vakuf, to the bottom of that page, number 27. We can see that Samir -- can you just tell us who was elected, so I get the pronunciation right.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: In Donji Vakuf constituency?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have a problem here, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You don't have it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. Because obviously if -- if you hadn't made a -- or not a mistake, but if you hadn't mentioned the name that you mentioned --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- I wouldn't have noticed. But actually, after page 20, at the bottom of which there is the constituency of the municipality of Donji Vakuf --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We've missed out the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- we missed -- at least, I missed the next eight pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour would. But you should have page 21. And we then go from 21 to 29.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I don't have page 21. I have page 29.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, it's my fault. I'll add that in. When I was selecting the pages for copy, I obviously made a mistake. But anyhow, perhaps the witness can just tell us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: A gentleman by the name of Samir Sutkovic was elected in Donji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Samir Sutkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Samir?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sutkovic. Your Honour, that's "S" with the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm making a correction. Samir Sutkovic. And he was representing the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll provide the extra page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. We should, in everybody's bundle, go to page 29.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And sir, can you find Kljuc? And do we see that a Serb called Rajko Kalabic was elected?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: I have found Kljuc constituency, Rajko Kalabic, candidate of the Serb Democratic Party, and he was elected.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if we go to the next page, Kotor Varos, there a Serb, Nedjeljko Djekanovic, was elected?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right, under 2, candidate of the Serb Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then can we go, sir -- if you could find Prijedor, which is on our page 38 -- 39, I'm sorry. There, I think, Mevludin Sejmenovic, a Muslim from Trnopolje, was elected on behalf of the SDA? That's number 74, sir, on the list.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Could you help me, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 1257, if you look at the page numbers in the upper, right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's -- the big number is 00497414.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you. [Interpretation] Prijedor constituency, that's right, Stojan Vracar.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think you'll find, sir, that it was Mevludin Sejmenovic who was elected. I agree it's very difficult to read on the photocopy.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right. It's barely legible, Sejmenovic, that's right, yes, and Marko Pavic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, they stood, and Mr. Sejmenovic won in the second round. Then could we look at the next constituency?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Sejmenovic, yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then if we look at the next constituency, Prnjavor, a Serb named Vidic was elected?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then --

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Dobrivoje Vidic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we come to your constituency, please, Sanski Most, which is number 80. I imagine, sir, it should be fairly close to Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I see it. So this is constituency 80.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And again, I think here there was a -- what we call a runoff vote with Nedjeljko Rasula from the SDS, and Hivzo Hodzic?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Hivzo Hodzic, and Nedjeljko Rasula was elected, and he stood for the Serb Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then if we turn over -- sorry, if you could find, sir, we go to page 44 next, where we come to Sipovo and Teslic.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Constituency 79, municipality of Sipovo.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter corrects herself, 89. Municipality of Sipovo.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Stevan Medic was elected.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the next constituency, Teslic?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Constituency number 90, municipality of Teslic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And again I think a Serb was elected?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Bosko Misic, that's right, from Teslic, was elected.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, sir. In fact, I think we appear to have made a mistake again on the copying, so there is one further thing I want us to look at.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to ask -- this is my error again. I've obviously made a mistake on the copying but there is some further pages at the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you find finally, sir - just to give the evidence and then you can put the document away - near the end, it says, "The national structure of elected deputies in the BH assembly." Does that show that in the Chamber of municipalities there were 43 Muslims, 40 Serbs, 24 Croats and three who described themselves as Yugoslavs? And that's on page 58 of the translation.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will make sure those extra two pages are given to Your Honour tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, after -- just -- actually, before I deal with what happened after those elections, as far as companies that were in Sanski Most were concerned, were they mainly state-owned?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: By the time of the elections in 1990, how many of them were privatised or semi-privatised?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: By 1990, there was no privatisation. These were all state-owned companies. Privatisation is only now going on, after the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And for the largest companies, companies that -- a company called Sip, S-I-P?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Sip Sana. That is a wood-processing company. It was the largest company in Sanski Most and it was the main factor of development of the municipality of Sanski Most. It had between 2.000 and 2.500 employees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, unless you require more information on these state-owned companies from the witness, may I suggest to you to read out to him the relevant paragraph from his statement and ask him to confirm it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think he need read the whole paragraph, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is this right? There was another large company called the 20th of October, which had about 1.100 people working for it?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then there was a factory called Kamengrad, which had 400 people working in a coal mine?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was a coal mine, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then a factory called Keramika, which was in the business of producing tiles, for 300 people -- I'm sorry, which had 300 people working for them?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That was Sanakeram.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I think there were other businesses in the construction industry, agriculture, and you had a lot of people working abroad.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, we've looked at the result of the elections that we saw. Mr. Hodzic, was he the President of the SDA party?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was, Mr. Hivzo Hodzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just to jump ahead, what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: He was unfortunately killed in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And at what stage was he killed in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning in the Sanski Most municipality, he was arrested in his apartment and he was detained in Betonirka. He was then supposed to be transferred to Manjaca, and during that transfer, he died because of the conditions under which he was transported -- transferred. This was on the 7th of July, 1992. So on the way, in this convoy, during the transfer towards Manjaca, he succumbed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, we saw that Mr. Rasula won the election. Was he the president of the SDS party?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Rasula, he was the president of the SDS party.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the HDZ, was that a gentleman named Mr. Tunic?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was. Ante Tunic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I deal with Sanski Most. We've seen that it was a mixed community really between Serbs and Muslims with a small proportion of Croats. Were there any ethnic tensions before the elections in 1990?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that all ethnicities, all nationalities in Sanski Most lived harmoniously side by side, so there were no interethnic tensions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was there intermarriage between the ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were many mixed marriages. And Sanski Most's surroundings were very much mixed, with different ethnicities that you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, the elections which took place. As far as the municipal assembly was concerned, did the SDS get 23 seats, the SDA 22, 7 seats for the SDP, 4 for the HDZ, and 4 for the Reform party?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, after the elections, what was the position in respect of the allocation of positions?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: After the elections, the parties negotiated regarding the positions in accordance with the results of the elections.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And were those negotiations successful in the allocation of the various positions?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: For the most -- for a number of most important positions in the municipality, the parties negotiated and they took those positions. But when it came to lower level positions, the positions in the judiciary, in the police, where mostly -- there were mostly Serb deputies and not so many Bosniaks and Croats --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Employees, not deputies.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: -- this is where the negotiations came upon obstacles.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just very briefly, if you can, in one sentence, what was the major obstacle to the successful outcome of the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: I can mention the police administration or the public security station, the police. There, there were more than 70 per cent of people employed. They were Serbs. They were policemen of Serb ethnicity. In the court, the judiciary, there were 70 per cent of employees who were of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, sir -- perhaps I can -- so is the answer that effectively the Serbs did not want to relinquish any positions there to other -- to members of other ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Then perhaps just before we break, I can deal with the other major positions. We've already dealt with Mr. Rasula. Did he become the president of the municipal assembly?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: After the elections, the SDS party won by a very small number of votes. Rasula took over the position of the president of the Municipal Assembly of Sanski Most. The president of the executive board was the candidate from the SDA, Mr. Karabik -- Mirsad Karabik [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Hodzic the deputy president of the assembly?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. He was the deputy president -- or rather, vice-president. He was a volunteer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And finally, on the police. Was the chief of police a man named Dragan Majkic, who was an SDS member, and the commander somebody called Enver Burnic, who was a member of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: When negotiations were held regarding the division of positions in the police administration, or rather, the public security station of Sanski Most, there were -- there was a lot of discord. And finally, the SDA yielded the position of the chief of the public security station, to which the candidate Dragan Majkic was elected. And for the commander, the candidate of Bosniak ethnicity was elected, Enver Burnic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I think in the case of Mr. Burnic as with Mr. Hodzic, was he also later killed?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Burnic. I apologise. It's Mr. Burnic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's my pronunciation. But was he -- can you just deal with this: Was he later killed as well in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC
utterances.text: Immediately in the beginning of the aggression on the Sanski Most municipality, he was arrested among the first ones and he was detained in Betonirka. And he disappeared. He has not been found to date. From the premises of the police administration, he was seen by some people as being driven to Manjaca -- in the direction of Manjaca and that he was returned. I mean, some other camp prisoners who were driven in lorries.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know what time you're going on to today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have another ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then I think someone else who joined -- or came to join the municipal Secretariat for Defence, apart from two people who were SDS members, was a man named Nedjeljko Anicic.
